implementation_notes: C++ has the pieces but not the pattern: std::map (or std::multimap when duplicates are legal) keeps the pending window ordered by sequence number, std::condition_variable::wait_for supplies the gap timeout, and a mutex-protected cursor drives the release. std::priority_queue is sufficient when only the head is ever inspected, but the map's ability to erase an arbitrary sequence number is what makes 'reject old', 'duplicate sequence' and capacity eviction cheap. Asio-based services replace the timed wait with a steady_timer whose expiry runs the same policy without changing the window structure.
pitfalls: std::condition_variable::wait_for can wake spuriously, so the predicate must re-check the window; the gap deadline also has to be recomputed from a deadline rather than re-armed per iteration.
Calling the consumer's deliver() while holding the window mutex serialises delivery and deadlocks if the consumer re-enters the resequencer.
std::priority_queue cannot erase a delivered, rejected or evicted element; use std::map when the window needs arbitrary removal.
An unordered_map cannot serve as the window: the head of the pending set is exactly what the cursor needs.
